title: Suet crust pastry
subtitle: The dense, filling pastry for steamed puddings and meat pie lids
excerpt: Suet crust is made with self-raising flour and shredded suet, brought together with cold water to a soft, spongy dough. Unlike shortcrust, it is not rubbed in, the suet melts into the dough during cooking, producing a thick, yielding texture suited to steamed puddings and steak pudding basins.
sourceNotes: Suet crust pastry is documented in Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136. The 2:1 self-raising flour to suet ratio has been the British standard for steamed puddings and meat-in-pastry for over 150 years.

recipe.yieldDescription: Enough to line and lid a 1.2 litre pudding basin
recipe.freezeNotes: Suet crust does not freeze well before cooking. Freeze the finished, cooked pudding instead.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Use immediately; suet crust toughens if it sits before cooking.

glossaryTerms.definition: Hard white fat from around the kidneys of beef or mutton, sold shredded in packets. Vegetable suet is available as a substitute. The high melting point of suet is what gives suet crust its unique texture after steaming.

content.text: Suet crust is the pastry of steamed steak pudding and jam roly-poly. Unlike shortcrust, it is not about tenderness through cold fat and minimal handling. The
melts during the long steam, making the pastry dense and filling rather than crisp. It must be made quickly and cooked immediately.
250 g self-raising flour, 125 g shredded suet, ½ tsp salt, 8 to 10 tbsp cold water. For a sweet version (jam roly-poly, spotted dick), add 1 tbsp caster sugar.
Mix the flour, suet, and salt together in a bowl until the suet is evenly distributed.
Add cold water, a tablespoon at a time, mixing with a knife. Stop when the dough is soft and slightly sticky but holds together. It should be noticeably softer than shortcrust dough.
Turn onto a floured surface and use immediately. Roll gently to 8 to 10 mm thick for pudding basins and steamed puddings.

Cut off one third of the dough for the lid. Roll the remaining two thirds into a circle wide enough to line the basin with a 2 cm overhang. Press the pastry into the greased basin, working out any air pockets. Fill with the prepared filling, then roll the reserved dough into a disc to fit the top. Dampen the overhanging pastry edges with water, fold up and press onto the lid to seal. Cover with buttered baking paper and a layer of foil, tied with string.
Vegetable suet is widely available and works in all suet crust recipes. The flavour is milder than beef suet and the texture in the finished crust is almost identical.
